title: Australasian Applied Statistics Conference 2026
text: We would like to cordially invite you to Queensland for the Australasian Applied Statistics Conference 2026 (AASC2026) to be held from the 30th November to the 4th December 2026 at the Mantra Mooloolaba Beach on the Sunshine Coast. AASC2026 is for anyone passionate about real-world data analysis, providing opportunities to exchange ideas in all areas of applied statistics, as well as encouraging networking and collaboration. Whether you are a student, researcher, industry representative, or simply have a keen interest in anything related to data science, AASC2026 will provide plenty of opportunities to learn, engage, share, and connect with fellow data science enthusiasts in a friendly and welcoming setting.

We are excited to announce the following pre-conference workshops will take place on Monday the \(30^{\text{th}}\) November.


Full-day ASReml-R Workshop

This one-day workshop will focus on modelling complex variance-covariance structures in biological experiments using ASReml-R. ASReml-R is a statistical library in R that fits linear mixed models using REML methodology. This workshop will cover key variance structures for random effects and residuals, including spatial, repeated measures, multivariate, and multi-environment models, with applications drawn from agricultural and medical research contexts.
The workshop is oriented toward practical analysis of real datasets. Participants are expected to have prior familiarity with linear mixed model methodology and R, and should bring their own laptop with R and ASReml-R pre-installed. A training ASReml-R license will be provided.

Morning (4 sessions)

Introduction & Linear Mixed Model Refresher
Brief ASReml-R orientation, mixed model theory, fixed vs random effects, and REML estimation.
Variance Structures in ASReml-R
The core topic considering diagonal, correlation, unstructured, and factor analytic structures.
Spatial Variance Structures
Modelling residual spatial correlation in field trials using AR1\(\times\)AR1 structures.
Repeated Measures & Random Regression
Modelling correlations over time, using simple or complex approaches.



Afternoon (3 sessions)

Bivariate & Multivariate Models
Random effects and residual correlation structures between responses.
Multi-Environment Trials & Factor Analytic Models
G\(\times\)E interaction, factor analytic variance structures, and extensions to other contexts.
Expanding to Complex Structures
Modelling multi-stratum designs with multiple layers of correlation between random effects and residuals.

Dr. Salvador Gezan (VSNi)

From fishing trips to stock indicators: An introduction to fisheries catch rate standardisation in R

This interactive half-day workshop will introduce you to the standardisation of fisheries catch rates (CPUE) using R. You’ll work with a realistic simulated catch-and-effort dataset and step through the key stages and decisions of a CPUE standardisation workflow, including:

Filtering data
Considering model structure and covariates
Fitting simple CPUE linear models, and
Generating annual predictions

You’ll gain an applied understanding of why catch rates often need to be standardised, how to fit and interpret simple CPUE standardisation models in R, how to generate and visualise annual standardised indices, and how those indices are used within a stock assessment context. We’ll explore some conceptual conundrums, like targeting behaviour and fishing efficiency. The content will focus on practical modelling decisions and reproducible analysis.
The workshop will be accessible to participants without a fisheries background. A basic understanding of R would be helpful.

Keynote #1 - Dr. Petra Kuhnert


Chair: Angela Anderson

Irresponsible use of AI is a Crime Scene: sifting through the slop to deliver responsible AI solutions


Dr. Petra Kuhnert



Abstract


Artificial Intelligence (AI) is moving at a rapid pace, shaping decisions across sectors and communities. As a result, the number of paper submissions to leading AI venues has surged. For example, in 2025, a little over 71,000 papers were submitted to the main research track of five of the top machine learning conferences, representing a 32% increase since 24 and a 10-fold increase from ten years ago. This rise in volume is becoming increasingly difficult to manage and consume in the academic community. Alongside genuine advances, there is also work that is incremental, overly tuned to curated benchmarks, weakly evidenced or even AI-generated without adequate verification.


If we want AI research and deployed systems that are trusted, robust and transparent, we need a forensic lens on how AI and its underlying analytics are developed and evaluated. For me, Statistics provides that lens, yet it can be sidelined in the rush to publish AI and deploy.


In this talk, I use the metaphor of a crime scene to describe AI crime: errors in predictions, uncertainty and inference that lead to poor decisions and in high-stakes settings can translate into real-world harm. I outline what Responsible, Application-Driven AI (RAD-AI) looks like in practice, and the statistical checks and incentives that help prevent failure modes and AI crime before it reaches the field. I will illustrate these ideas with work we are developing with stakeholders to produce a trusted AI crop growth model.


We would not cut corners at a crime scene, so why would we allow crime to happen with AI!




Biography


Dr. Petra Kuhnert is a Senior Principal Research Scientist at CSIRO and an expert at the intersection of statistics and machine learning. Her work develops methodology for risk-based decision-making in environmental and agricultural applications where she develops methods that are fit for purpose, relevant to the question at hand, and usable by decision-makers.


Her work, particularly supporting Great Barrier Reef decision-making, has been recognised through awards including 1st Runner Up (APAC Women in AI Innovator of the Year, 2023) and the APAC Women in AI Award for Environment and Biodiversity (2023).


A key contribution to AI-driven decision-making is her award-winning software Vizumap, an R package that helps users understand and communicate uncertainty on maps.


More recently, her focus has included machine-learning emulators to speed up slow-running physical system models, Bayesian methods for decision support, and approaches that use geospatial data (e.g., remote sensing) to improve prediction of terrestrial environmental and agricultural processes. Her previous roles include Associate Science Director for University Engagement and Group Leader of the Statistical Machine Learning Group in CSIRO’s Data61.


She has co-authored 100+ journal articles, with 6,000+ citations and a Google Scholar h-index of 30+. Her collaborations span leading government departments, universities and industry.

Genstat Markdown: Reproducible Research with Genstat


James Curran



Abstract


Reproducible research ensures that scientific findings can be independently verified by others using the same data and methods. Markdown plays a key role in supporting reproducibility by allowing researchers to combine code, results, and narrative text in a clear, lightweight format. Tools like R Markdown or Jupyter Notebooks use Markdown to embed executable code alongside explanations and outputs, making it easy to document workflows, share analyses, and regenerate results consistently across different environments.


Genstat is a statistical software package designed for data analysis, particularly in biometrical research and applications. Many users know it through its user-friendly interface. However, it also It offers a powerful scripting language.


In this talk I will describe a collaborative project between students and staff at the University of Auckland and VSNi Ltd, that allows Genstat to be used in conjunction with R Markdown to provide flexible reproducible research capability to the Genstat user community.




Biography


My research focuses on statistical problems in forensic science, particularly the interpretation of DNA, and trace evidence. More broadly, I enjoy developing statistical methods and practical tools motivated by real-world problems.

Pizzas, Biometry and the 5Rs


Mario D’Antuono



Abstract


In 2008, at the Australasian Genstat Users Association (AGUA) meeting, then known as the Genstat Conference in Marysville, Victoria, I presented a controversial paper on my forthcoming e-book entitled “Biometry: The 5Rs”.


The paper was controversial because it presented an argument that in 5 simple lines of code using the R Statistical System (denoted by R) usually in the form of a function call, I could address a task such as the generation of a near-optimal design, or a statistical analysis. These 5 lines can be recursive and hence can call other functions within a function (a nested approach). The approach was stimulated by the work of Karl Broman at the time and his 3Rs (Reproducible Research with R).


In 2019, I retired from the Department of Agriculture, Western Australia. It has taken 7 years for me to find the time and the energy to complete the e-book. The free R software to handle the above has developed to be able to treat many of the common problems in agricultural research.


We illustrate two published examples from the literature, which are case-studies in the e-book; the first involves the construction of a near-optimal p-rep design, and the second, a spatial linear mixed model analysis. We compare the results from the University of Wollongong R packages dwreml-R and odw-R (soon to be released on GitHub) with other software such as CycDesign, speed-R, and DiGGer-R for near-optimal design generation, and asreml-R and Echidna for linear mixed modelling.




Biography


Mario worked as a biometrician in the Biometrics Unit of the WA Dept of Agriculture (now known as DPIRD) from 1977 to 2019. He was President of the Australasian Region of the International Biometric Society (IBS-AR) 2011-2012. He was a long-time Genstat user and was heavily involved in the Genstat conference, Busselton December 2002, and the IBS-AR meeting held in December 2013 at Mandurah, WA.

A modified PQL method for genetic analysis of binary variables


Arthur Gilmour



Abstract


In plant and animal breeding, there is the need to estimate breeding values for binary traits such as lamb survival and presence/absence of disease. For such traits, the average incidence is often outside [0.2, 0.8] and it varies with known fixed effects and covariates. Animal breeders commonly assume the binary trait is based on an underlying normal liability exceeding a threshold. PQL (pseudo quasi-likelihood), an extension of GLM to include random effects in the linear model, is commonly used to analyse such data and predict breeding values, but is known to underestimate the heritability when fitting an animal model. It iterates using a working variable \(\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{\eta} + (\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{\mu})/\delta\), where \(\mathbf{\eta}\) is the prediction on the liability scale (\(\mathbf{X\beta}+\mathbf{Zu}\)), \(\mathbf{y}\) is binary outcome, \(\mathbf{\mu} = f(\mathbf{\eta})\) is predicted mean on the probability scale, \(\delta\) is the derivative of the probit link function \(f(\eta)\), \(\mathbf{X}\) is the design matrix for fixed effects (\(\mathbf{\beta}\)) and \(\mathbf{Z}\) is the design matrix for random effects (\(\mathbf{u}\)). The linear model,\(\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{X\beta} + \mathbf{Zu} + \mathbf{e}\) is fitted with weights \(δ^2/\)var(\(y\)), var(\(y\)) is \(\mu(1-\mu)\). The mPQL model, in the simplest case, calculates \(\mathbf{\eta} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{\beta}\), leading to changes in \(\mu\) and \(\delta\), and necessitates estimating a dispersion factor when fitting the linear model (which is unchanged). My recommendation when using mPQL is first to fit the model on the probability scale, note the mean (\(p\)), calculate the heritability (\(h_o^2\)), the dispersion factor \(((1 - h_o^2)\) and predict an approximate heritability for the liability scale using \(h_l^2 = h_o^2 p(1-p)/z^2\). Then, fit the mPQL model using the dispersion factor. mPQL is available in Echidna (EchidnaMMS.org)




Biography


Arthur Gilmour worked for NSW Agriculture as a biometrician from 1970 to 2008. He is currently contracted part time to VSN International to support ASReml.

ggincerta: An R package for Uncertainty Visualisation with a Layered Grammar of Graphics


Maggie Ma



Abstract


A key challenge in spatial visualisation is the simultaneous communication of estimated values and their associated uncertainties, as visual channels are occupied by spatial structure, leaving limited capacity to encode additional information. We developed ggincerta, an R package that extends the layered grammar of graphics implemented in ggplot2, to facilitate the visualisation of uncertainty in spatial data. Through its native integration with ggplot2, ggincerta enables users to leverage the full flexibility of the grammar of graphics to create complex and customised visualisations through simpler and more consistent workflows in spatial and more general data settings. In addition to reproducing existing uncertainty visualisation techniques, the package introduces new approaches, including the dual map, a visualisation designed to support selective attention between estimated values and their associated uncertainties. We demonstrate the capabilities of ggincerta through several case studies, illustrating how the package can be used to create informative and visually effective maps that communicate both estimates and uncertainty, while also highlighting relevant technical details and visual features. By integrating uncertainty visualisation directly into the ggplot2 ecosystem and expanding the range of available uncertainty displays, ggincerta provides a flexible and powerful framework for researchers and practitioners working with spatial and other information-rich data.




Biography


Maggie Ma is a PhD student in Statistics at the Australian National University. Her research focuses on statistical graphics, spatial data visualisation, and the communication of uncertainty. She is currently developing the R package ggincerta, which extends the ggplot2 framework with specialised layers and scales for visualising uncertainty in geospatial data.

torch-openreml: a PyTorch-based framework for flexible linear mixed-effects modelling


Patrick Li



Abstract


We introduce torch-openreml, a PyTorch-based Python library under active early development for fitting linear mixed-effects models using the Average Information Restricted Maximum Likelihood (AI-REML) algorithm. The library represents covariance models as compositional computation graphs, where complex covariance structures are constructed by combining modular components through algebraic operations.


Within this framework, model parameters can be fixed, estimated, or transformed, with analytical gradients provided where possible and PyTorch automatic differentiation used for general cases. The AI-REML solver exploits common covariance structures to improve computational efficiency and benefits from PyTorch support for CPUs, GPUs, and other accelerators.


Although currently in an early alpha stage, torch-openreml supports a wide range of linear mixed-effects modelling applications, such as multi-environment trial analysis, spatial modelling, and genomic prediction. It enables rapid prototyping of novel covariance models without requiring manual gradient derivation, providing an extensible platform for modern mixed-effects modelling.




Biography


Dr Weihao (Patrick) Li is a Postdoctoral Research Fellow at the Research School of Finance, Actuarial Studies and Statistics, Australian National University. He holds a PhD in Statistics from Monash University. His research in the Analytics for the Australian Grains Industry (AAGI) project focuses on machine learning, image analytics, and plant phenotyping.

One Workflow, Many Questions: A Unified Workflow for Statistical Modelling in the Age of AI


Kathrin Schemann



Abstract


Applied statisticians increasingly work across diverse modelling paradigms, each with distinct assumptions, methods, and reporting requirements. At the same time, the rapid emergence of AI tools creates opportunities to improve efficiency while raising important questions about transparency, reproducibility, and statistical rigor.


This presentation introduces a practical, software-agnostic workflow developed at the Statistical Consulting Unit of the Sydney Informatics Hub, The University of Sydney. The workflow provides a unified framework for addressing descriptive, predictive, and causal modelling objectives while maintaining focus on fundamental statistical principles and research context. The framework follows a shared structure that begins with clearly defining the research question, identifying variables of interest, documenting assumptions, and developing a transparent analysis plan. Key components include study design, bias assessment, variable selection, interaction assessment, model evaluation, interpretation, and communication of results. The presentation also examines how AI can be integrated throughout the analytical process, supporting tasks such as planning, coding, documentation, model implementation, diagnostic review, and reporting. Within the workflow, AI is positioned as a tool to augment—not replace—statistical expertise, subject-matter knowledge, and professional judgment.


By combining established statistical principles with structured opportunities for AI augmentation, the workflow provides a consistent approach to applied statistical practice across modelling objectives, supporting more transparent, reproducible, efficient, and impactful research.




Biography


Kathrin is a Senior Statistical Consultant and leads the operations of the Statistical Consulting Unit at the Sydney Informatics Hub (University of Sydney). With 15+ years of broad, applied experience in academia and public health, she develops practical workflows to empower researchers with robust statistical skills, particularly in optimising analytical design for higher impact research.

Nested-factorial treatment models: types, their uses and examples


Chris Brien



Abstract


Most commonly factorial experiments involve several crossed treatment factors and the treatment model includes terms for all possible combinations of the treatment factors. However, treatment models that employ nested treatment factors are beneficial in a number of situations and could be used more often. Applicable situations include those in which (i) treatment factors are intrinsically nested, (ii) treatments involve one or more factors plus a control and (iii) treatments have been systematically allocated and/or are pseudoreplicated. Four basic types of nested factors that start with a single nesting factor are (i) one nested factor, (ii) multiple, crossed, nested factors, (iii) multiple, independent, nested factors, and (iv) a hierarchy of multiple, nested factors. Examples involving the different situations and types of nesting will be presented. Constructing the factors using the R package dae (Brien, 2026, https://cran.r-project.org/package=dae) will be described and the properties of the models discussed for the examples via their anatomies produced using dae.

My main interests are in experiment design and linear mixed model analysis, especially for multiphase experiments. In the last 10 years, the design and analysis of plant phenotyping data has become a particular focus. I also maintain three R packages on CRAN.

Fitting Large Genomic Models: Computational Strategies and Approximations within the Linear Mixed Model Framework


Dr. Salvador Gezan



Abstract


As genomic datasets grow larger, substantial statistical and computational challenges arise when analysing single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) data. Such data are widely used in Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS), Polygenic Risk Score (PRS) analyses, and genome-wide prediction models. Depending on the field and context, it is common to encounter datasets containing millions of SNPs and hundreds of thousands of genotyped individuals. Fitting even the simplest linear mixed model at this scale is computationally demanding, requiring the handling of large genomic matrices and the estimation of a large number of marker effects. Statistical and mathematical techniques such as Cholesky decomposition, eigen-transformation, Singular Value Decomposition, and low-rank matrix approximations provide practical solutions for fitting these models and obtaining the required effects and predictions. This talk will present key mathematical details, illustrations, and practical guidelines for addressing large-scale genomic analyses in plant and animal breeding.




Biography


Salvador Gezan is a statistician and quantitative geneticist with over 20 years of experience, currently serving as a Statistical Genetics Consultant at VSN International. He specialises in mixed models and their application to biological problems, supporting agricultural, forestry, and aquaculture breeding programmes through the analysis of phenotypic and genotypic data, the development of breeding strategies, and the implementation of genomic selection in operational breeding programmes. He began his career at Rothamsted Research, was an Associate Professor at the University of Florida, and has delivered ASReml workshops globally. Dr. Gezan has over 160 peer-reviewed publications and is a co-author of Statistical Methods in Biology: Design and Analysis of Experiments and Regression.

Predicting Cotton Fibre Performance using GWAS Summary Statistics


Qian Feng



Abstract


Genomic prediction (GP) refers to the prediction of individual’s phenotypes using genome-wide information. In humans, GP has contributed substantially to the development of precision medicine, while in animal and plant breeding it has accelerated genetic gain by enabling earlier and more accurate selection. Traditional GP methods rely on individual-level genotype and phenotype data, which are often subject to privacy, ownership and data sharing restrictions. Recently, summary-statistics-based methods have emerged for GP by leveraging genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics and linkage disequilibrium information from a reference population. These approaches avoid the need of individual-level data and have been widely applied in human genetics. However, their application in plant breeding, including cotton, remains very limited. Here, we investigate the feasibility of summary-statistics-based genomic prediction using a large-scale cotton dataset collected over 40 year-site combinations in central-eastern Australia. Both genotype and phenotype data are available for this dataset, enabling the computation of GWAS summary statistics and a direct comparison between conventional Genomic Best Linear Unbiased Prediction (GBLUP) and a summary-statistics-based BLUP approach. Our empirical results show that the two methods achieve comparable prediction accuracy across multiple fibre yield and quality traits, consistent with theoretical expectations. We further evaluate how the choice of reference population and GWAS summary statistics information influences prediction performance. These results demonstrate the potential of summary-statistics-based GP in cotton and suggest that this approach could enable the use of larger, more diverse publicly available datasets to support the development of better cotton varieties.




Biography


Qian Feng is a CERC research fellow at CSIRO Agriculture and Food Unit. Her current research focuses on designing and implementing statistical methods to accelerate the breeding of Australian rain-grown cotton. She also interests in detecting evolutionary processes from pathogen and human genomes, including the recombination identification with hidden Markov models.





14:45-15:00


Protein Advantage for Mungbean in Australia


Jodine O’Connor



Abstract


The growing emphasis on plant-based diets and the increasing demand for protein have brought pulse grains into sharp focus. As the second-largest exporter of pulse grains globally, Australia is uniquely positioned to meet this rising demand. To maintain market share and leverage the growing interest in plant-based protein, the Grains Research and Development Corporation (GRDC) and Agriculture Victoria have initiated a national project aimed at exploring innovative strategies to support and expand this vital industry. The project focuses on six pulse crops: mungbean, chickpea, lupin, lentil, faba bean and field pea. To date, historical varieties for each crop have been evaluated across Australia’s major pulse growing regions. These trials span 33 sites across five states, conducted in 2024 and 2025. With demand to meeting new markets, a challenge arises for breeding varieties that achieve both high yield and desirable protein levels. Therefore, a statistical methodology is proposed with a protein advantage metric. Using available mungbean data, a multi-environment, across-year bivariate analysis was performed for three sites in QLD and NSW. This analysis examined yield and protein content within a bivariate linear mixed model framework, extended to incorporate multi-environment data. The framework also included spatial modelling for each trial and factor analytic modelling to allow for heterogeneous genetic covariance across trials. The bivariate analysis revealed a strong negative genetic correlation between yield and protein content across all environments. The protein advantage metric was obtained by using genotype deviations from the regression line between protein and yield. When plotted, varieties with a positive protein advantage or a negative advantage are clearly identified. This information provides valuable insights for growers and pulse breeders to select varieties that align with targeted market traits (e.g. protein) and production goals in Australia.




Biography


My career began in animal breeding and genetics before progressing into plant breeding. I enjoy experimental design and analysis of Multiple Environment Trials (MET) incorporating pedigree information across many commercial crops using ASReml-R. My interests include pedigree analysis, image analysis, marker data analysis, data management and working with industry to streamline research outcomes.

Identifying cellular relationships in finely annotated spatial transcriptomics data


Ellis Patrick



Abstract


Recent cell-resolution spatial transcriptomics technologies enable whole-transcriptome profiling of millions of individual cells within intact tissues, creating unprecedented opportunities to study how cellular organisation varies across development, health and disease. However, the same resolution that makes these data biologically powerful also makes them analytically fragile. Although these assays target approximately 20,000 genes, each cell typically contains only a sparse sample of detected transcripts, with measurements also contaminated by transcript diffusion, imperfect segmentation and cell overlap. This makes expression estimates uncertain and can destabilise fine-grained cell labels. Fine-grained labels can also fragment the data into rare populations for which spatial associations are difficult to estimate precisely. Inference on spatial organisation is further complicated by correlation at multiple scales, arising from cohort design, tissue sampling and the spatial arrangement of cells within structured anatomical regions. Together, measurement error, annotation uncertainty and dependence can produce unstable estimates and reduced power for detecting meaningful spatial relationships.


In this talk, I will present approaches developed by my team to address these challenges in high-dimensional spatial omics data. Using hierarchical modelling, cluster-robust variance estimation, bootstrapping and weighting strategies, we developed more robust and powerful tests for spatial association under annotation uncertainty and multiscale dependence. These methods support inference across cell-cell association testing, proximity-associated gene programs, rare-cell localisation and multicellular tissue architecture, providing a framework for extracting reliable biological signal from sparse, contaminated and correlated spatial omics data.




Biography


Ellis Patrick is an Associate Professor in the School of Mathematics and Statistics at the University of Sydney and Cluster Lead of Bioinformatics in the Sydney Precision Data Science Centre. His research develops statistical methods and software for spatial omics and other emerging biomedical technologies, helping researchers better understand human disease.

A Location-Scale Linked Autoregressive Moving Average Model for Wind Direction Time Series Data


Piumi Perera



Abstract


Modelling long-term wind direction time series data poses several challenges, including the circular nature of the observations, temporal processes operating at multiple scales, and the need to jointly capture both mean direction and variability in the presence of serial dependence. Motivated by hourly wind direction observations collected between 2013 and 2016 from a Bureau of Meteorology station in Broome, Western Australia, we propose a location-scale linked autoregressive moving average (LSLARMA) model that prioritises interpretability and data generation. The proposed framework adopts a two-stage approach, comprising a location-scale regression applied to transformed wind direction, followed by a (seasonal) ARMA model fitted to the resulting quantile residuals to capture remaining serial dependence. Application of the LSLARMA model reveals clear annual, monthly, and diurnal patterns in both the mean and dispersion of wind direction. In addition, the model can generate realistic synthetic time series that reproduce key features of the observed wind direction data, while compared with alternative single stage approaches the proposed method delivers improved performance and greater interpretability of the underlying temporal processes.




Biography


Piumi Perera is a PhD student in Statistics at the Australian National University. Their research focuses primarily on modelling circular responses and environmental data. 





16:00-16:15


Cross trial analysis of rotation by environment interaction in the Western Australian Farming Systems project


Ben Nestor



Abstract


The Western Australian Farming Systems (WAFS) project involves ongoing trials comparing four-year standard and diverse cropping rotations under two nitrogen supply levels (low and high). Trials are located across three WA cropping environments: Northampton (northern, medium rainfall), Merredin (eastern, low rainfall), and Lake Grace (southern, medium rainfall). Rotations include combinations of cereals, canola, grain legumes, manured legumes, multi-species, and fallow with different phasings of rotations. A multi-environment trial (MET) analysis was performed to investigate rotation x environment interactions, with environment defined as the combination of location and nitrogen treatment. The relative performance of each rotation was compared across environments using gross profit margins from three years of rotations as the response variable in a factor analytic model. The best linear unbiased predictions were compared across rotations to identify rotation types that were most profitable in different environments and rotation types that gave more consistent profits across environments. This analysis demonstrates a novel application of MET analysis on cropping rotation trials, providing insights into the effects of rotation and nitrogen treatment across different WA agricultural environments.




Biography


I completed a PhD in plant bioinformatics at the University of Western Australia in 2024 and joined DPIRD as a Biometrics Research Scientist later that year. At DPIRD, I have contributed to a range of agricultural, horticultural, and rangeland research projects and my work generally involves trial analyses and experimental design, multi-environment trial analyses, and multivariate analyses.

A quantitative framework for dissecting genotype by environment interactions driving crop yield variability


Stephanie Brunner



Abstract


Climate change magnifies unpredictable environmental patterns, threatening global crop yields. A wide range of approaches exist to assess varieties across environments through mixed linear models with latent or environmental variables. However, the underlying causes of these genotype by environment interactions (GEIs) remain unexplored. Understanding how genetic and environmental factors interact to drive yield variation is critical for breeding resilient crops. This research develops a framework to investigate the genetic and environmental drivers of GEI to help inform crop breeding decisions. Modelling plant growth for biological discovery

Abstract


High-throughput plant phenotyping platforms, such as those in the Australian Plant Phenomics Network, generate dense, repeated measurements of plant growth over time. These methods can accommodate nonlinear and irregular growth patterns directly from the data, while still yielding interpretable summaries such as growth rate, timing of key developmental transitions, and genotype- or treatment-level variation. Gaussian processes further provide a natural measure of uncertainty around these estimates, which is valuable when growth trajectories are noisy or unevenly sampled. We present this as a complementary approach to mechanistic modelling, rather than a replacement for it. Statistical characterisation of growth trajectories can help identify patterns that are worth investigating mechanistically, flagging where and when a genotype or treatment departs from expected growth, for example. Because these methods do not require a model to be fitted individually to each genotype or treatment, they are also well suited to the scale of modern phenomics platforms. In this way, statistical modelling offers a practical route to turning large-scale phenotypic data into biological insight.

A Statistical Framework for Data Streams

Are such concerns less important given the semi-quantitative nature of BOTANAL data, which rely on subjective ratings calibrated via fitted relationships between scores and observed dry matter?


This paper examines these issues and discusses the implications. In summary, averaging the quadrats is acceptable if skewness is mild/moderate with the quadrat distribution not biasing the mean severely, particularly given the subjectiveness of the data. However, if skewness is severe then apply the appropriate transformation (e.g. log transformation).

Kernel Propagation of Gradient Boosted Margins for Spatio-temporal Forecasting

Abstract

Abstract

Abstract


Artificial Intelligence (AI) is moving at a rapid pace, shaping decisions across sectors and communities. As a result, the number of paper submissions to leading AI venues has surged. For example, in 2025, a little over 71,000 papers were submitted to the main research track of five of the top machine learning conferences, representing a 32% increase since 24 and a 10-fold increase from ten years ago. This rise in volume is becoming increasingly difficult to manage and consume in the academic community. Alongside genuine advances, there is also work that is incremental, overly tuned to curated benchmarks, weakly evidenced or even AI-generated without adequate verification.


If we want AI research and deployed systems that are trusted, robust and transparent, we need a forensic lens on how AI and its underlying analytics are developed and evaluated. For me, Statistics provides that lens, yet it can be sidelined in the rush to publish AI and deploy.

For such traits, the average incidence is often outside [0.2, 0.8] and it varies with known fixed effects and covariates. Animal breeders commonly assume the binary trait is based on an underlying normal liability exceeding a threshold. PQL (pseudo quasi-likelihood), an extension of GLM to include random effects in the linear model, is commonly used to analyse such data and predict breeding values, but is known to underestimate the heritability when fitting an animal model. It iterates using a working variable \(\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{\eta} + (\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{\mu})/\delta\), where \(\mathbf{\eta}\) is the prediction on the liability scale (\(\mathbf{X\beta}+\mathbf{Zu}\)), \(\mathbf{y}\) is binary outcome, \(\mathbf{\mu} = f(\mathbf{\eta})\) is predicted mean on the probability scale, \(\delta\) is the derivative of the probit link function \(f(\eta)\), \(\mathbf{X}\) is the design matrix for fixed effects (\(\mathbf{\beta}\)) and \(\mathbf{Z}\) is the design matrix for random effects (\(\mathbf{u}\)). Across the Australian Plant Phenomics Network, drone phenotyping data are collected by different operators (network nodes), across multiple sites and years. These data are comparable only if every team collects, calibrates, and processes them the same way. The Airborne Phenomics Excellence project found that when operators repeat a drone flight or fly a shared target, results disagree, and the dominant, fixable cause is process, not sensors. The variance lived in field and processing procedure, and in whether the agreed method was written down, current, and followed. This presentation describes our response: managing scientific protocols the way software teams manage code, and then testing statistically whether they work.


Procedures live in a shared version-controlled repository, are revised through reviewed pull requests, locked as a published read-only wiki that teams follow in the field, and issued as tagged, citable releases, giving every dataset a permanent record of the method it was collected under.


But writing protocols down does not prove they deliver the comparability the network depends on. Conventional significance testing answers this poorly: failing to reject a difference is not evidence of equivalence, and with large pixel samples trivial differences become “significant”. In a controlled validation campaign, we frame cross-sensor calibration as a formal equivalence problem, deriving an equivalence bound and applying two one-sided tests (TOST) for mean reflectance, then assessing distributional equivalence (quantile TOST, Wasserstein distance, variance ratios) and a multivariate, classifier-based effect size across the visible-near-infrared and shortwave-infrared regions.


The result is a per-wavelength verdict (equivalent, non-equivalent, or inconclusive) showing where a procedure works and where recalibration is needed, a practical way to control variance and bias between operators, sites, and years that recur in multi-year, multi-site monitoring.





09:50-10:05


Integrating Spatial Data and On-Farm Experimentation to Analyse Wheat Variety Performance in Western Australia


Sandra Tanz



Abstract


On-farm experimentation (OFE) provides an opportunity to evaluate crop performance under commercial farming conditions while capturing the spatial variability inherent in production systems. However, this variability also presents statistical challenges for experimental design and analysis.


This pilot study investigates the integration of spatial data with large-scale OFE to better understand wheat variety performance across five grower-managed sites in Western Australia. Each trial was established within commercial paddocks using strip trial designs aligned with historical production zones. Two core wheat varieties, Scepter (a widely grown commercial cultivar) and Dale (a near-release InterGrain line) were included at all sites, with additional varieties incorporated where locally relevant.


The study focuses on developing and evaluating statistical methods that account for spatial variation by defining pseudo-environments using both equally spaced zones and environmental covariates derived from soil and topographic information. Trial analyses incorporate additional spatial datasets, including elevation and NDVI time series from drone and satellite imagery, to better characterise environmental heterogeneity and genotype-by-environment interactions.


The project aims to develop robust, spatially aware workflows for OFE trial design and analysis, encompassing data cleaning, spatial gridding, pseudo-environment assignment, and linear mixed modelling to account for spatial variation across commercial paddocks. By integrating spatial data, environmental covariates, and modern statistical methods, this work demonstrates the potential of OFE to complement conventional small-plot variety trials, improve variety evaluation, support agronomic decision-making, and contribute to predictive breeding in commercial farming systems.




Biography


Sandra Tanz is a Research Data Scientist at Curtin University, where she develops statistical and spatial analysis methods for on-farm experimentation in cereal breeding. She has a background in plant molecular biology and applied data science, with research interests in spatial statistics, mixed models, remote sensing, and the integration of environmental data into agricultural decision-making.





10:05-10:20


Bivariate analysis of ratio component traits in horticultural breeding programs


Ky Mathews



Abstract


Ratio traits are commonly used in agriculture as selection indices for complex characteristics. For example, flavour characteristics in strawberry are measured as a ratio of total soluble sugars to acidity, the so-called “brix-to-acid ratio”. In macadamia, fertility is measured as a ratio of the number of self-pollinated to open-pollinated florets on a raceme. The distributional properties of these ratio traits are often non-normal and heteroscedastic. For breeding decisions, selection on the component traits is also of interest and each has its own genetic variance that is ignored when incorporated into a ratio trait. In this study, we demonstrate a bivariate mixed-model approach for repeated measures, multi-year datasets is possible. Further, ancestral information is included to enable selection for variety release and for parents in future breeding cycles. Compared with direct univariate analysis of the derived ratio, the bivariate approach retains information on the component traits, quantifies their genetic relationship, and provides more interpretable outputs for selection of candidate varieties and future parents.




Biography


Ky is a Principal Biometrician at the Queensland Department of Primary Industries. She applies state-of-the-art statistical methods in plant breeding and pre-breeding programs. She is particularly interested in experimental design, spatial analyses, modelling genotype-by-environment interaction and incorporating pedigree and marker data in the linear mixed model framework.





10:20-10:35


Modelling stability of irrigated cotton farming system soil organic carbon content and function


Pauline Ding



Abstract


Long-term changes in stocks and stability within irrigated cotton farming systems in semi-arid Australia is of great public interest. Soil organic carbon underpins nutrient cycling, soil structural stability, and ecosystem resilience, yet soil organic carbon responses to crop rotation and diversification in irrigated Vertosols remain uncertain.


In this project, archived soil samples were collected between 1995 and 2020 from a long-term farming systems experiment at the Australian Cotton Research Institute, Narrabri, NSW. Treatments included continuous cotton and cotton rotated with wheat, vetch, or faba bean under minimum tillage management. The experiment commenced in 1995 in the West Field with five cropping treatments replicated four times. The following year, 1996, three additional treatments added in adjacent East Field, where the cotton phase occurred 12 months latter than the West Field. Soil samples were collected at 30cm, 60cm and 90 cm depth and analysed using dry combustion and near-infrared spectroscopy. In this study, we use linear mixed model to fit multivariate long-term soil collections and evaluate long-term soil carbon dynamics in intensive agricultural systems. This is a joint work with CISRO Agriculture and Food.




Biography


Pauline is a Lecturer in Statistics at the University of Wollongong. She has a strong portfolio of interdisciplinary research in public health, medicine, and the social sciences. More recently, Pauline has developed a passion for agricultural soil studies, inspired by the 29 heads of cattle on the family farm.

text:
The organising committee is proud to announce the following keynote speakers for AASC2026.


Prof. Ben Hayes



Presentation Title

Bayesian or machine learning approaches: what works best for genomic prediction?

Abstract

The foundational paper for genomic prediction, predicting complex traits from genome wide DNA markers, was published in 2001. Since then, genomic prediction has been widely adopted in crop and livestock production, and in human genetics for prediction of disease risk. In this overview, statistical methodologies for genomic prediction are compared, and we then speculate on the future of genomic prediction methodologies.

Biography

Professor Hayes has extensive research experience in genetic improvement of livestock, crop, pasture and aquaculture species, with a focus on integration of genomic information into breeding programs, including leading many large scale projects which have successfully implemented genomic technologies in livestock and cropping industries. Author of more than 300 journal papers, including in Nature Genetics, Nature Reviews Genetics, and Science, contributing to statistical methodology for genomic, microbiome and metagenomic profile predictions, quantitative genetics including knowledge of genetic mechanisms underlying complex traits.



Prof. Margarita Moreno-Betancur



Presentation Title

Causal inference in health research

Abstract

The ultimate goal of medical and health research is to improve patient outcomes and population health. As a result, an overwhelming majority of clinical and public health research studies ask “causal” questions, concerning the effect of treatments, policies, behaviours and other exposures on health outcomes, even if often unadmitted. In many cases, especially in the current era of data deluge, these studies rely on observational (non-experimental) data to address causal questions. Unfortunately, for a long time the statistics discipline largely shunned the possibility of causal inference beyond randomised trials, and instead focused on the development of tools such as regression models without clarity regarding their usefulness and limitations for addressing the causal questions that substantive areas continued to ask. In recent decades, however, the discipline has seen the rise of a new area focused on determining the settings and approaches that could allow causal inference from observational data. This talk will first provide an overview of some of the fundamental contributions of this statistical area to enable and improve the study of causality in health research and then provide an overview of recent advances in the area seeking further to advance the statistical methods, teaching and practice.

Biography

Professor Margarita Moreno-Betancur is co-Director of the Clinical Epidemiology and Biostatistics Unit at the Melbourne Children’s campus. She established an internationally recognised hub of innovation and expertise in statistical methods for observational studies, supported by competitive fellowship and grant funding. Her team conducts methodological research in causal inference and missing data while contributing their expertise to health research studies. She is Chair of the Victorian Centre for Biostatistics leadership team, Scientific Lead of the LifeCourse platform of cohort studies, and Editor of the journal Epidemiology. She was awarded the Moran Medal by the Australian Academy of Science in 2025.



Associate Prof. Peter Dunn



Presentation Title

Modelling continuous data with exact zeros

Abstract

Statistical models for continuous data (e.g., linear regression) and discrete data (e.g., logistic regression) are commonly used. Continuous data with exact zeros, while less common, appear in many applications. In this talk, different models are discussed for modelling this type of data, with a focus on using Poisson-gamma models, which are Poisson sums of gamma distributions. Poisson-gamma distributions are part of the EDM family, so can be used for modelling within the generalised linear models (GLMs) framework. This means that the fitting, model selection and residual analysis tools familiar from GLMs also apply to GLMs fitted to continuous data with exact zeros.

Biography

Peter is an Associate Professor in Biostatistics at the University of the Sunshine Coast, and routinely teaches introductory statistics to over 500 students over two semesters each year.
Peter has over 110 peer-reviewed research publications, has prepared numerous R packages available on CRAN (including the tweedie package, with almost 1 million downloads from CRAN) and co-developed the Dunn-Smyth (or quantile) residuals used in statistical modelling. Peter has been invited to give presentations on the R statistical environment at conferences and workshops across Australia.
Peter won an Australian Office of Learning and Teaching Citation in 2012, a student prize at the 16th International Workshop on Statistical Modelling in Denmark, and the EJ Pitman Prize for student talks at the Australian Statistics Conference in 2002. He has also published two textbooks: Generalized Linear Models With Examples in R (Springer) and Scientific Research and Methodology (CRS Press; also available as a free interactive online textbook).



Dr. Petra Kuhnert



Presentation Title

Irresponsible use of AI is a Crime Scene: sifting through the slop to deliver responsible AI solutions

Abstract

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is moving at a rapid pace, shaping decisions across sectors and communities. As a result, the number of paper submissions to leading AI venues has surged. For example, in 2025, a little over 71,000 papers were submitted to the main research track of five of the top machine learning conferences, representing a 32% increase since 24 and a 10-fold increase from ten years ago. This rise in volume is becoming increasingly difficult to manage and consume in the academic community. Alongside genuine advances, there is also work that is incremental, overly tuned to curated benchmarks, weakly evidenced or even AI-generated without adequate verification.
If we want AI research and deployed systems that are trusted, robust and transparent, we need a forensic lens on how AI and its underlying analytics are developed and evaluated. For me, Statistics provides that lens, yet it can be sidelined in the rush to publish AI and deploy.
In this talk, I use the metaphor of a crime scene to describe AI crime: errors in predictions, uncertainty and inference that lead to poor decisions and in high-stakes settings can translate into real-world harm. I outline what Responsible, Application-Driven AI (RAD-AI) looks like in practice, and the statistical checks and incentives that help prevent failure modes and AI crime before it reaches the field. I will illustrate these ideas with work we are developing with stakeholders to produce a trusted AI crop growth model.
We would not cut corners at a crime scene, so why would we allow crime to happen with AI!

Biography

Dr. Petra Kuhnert is a Senior Principal Research Scientist at CSIRO and an expert at the intersection of statistics and machine learning. Her work develops methodology for risk-based decision-making in environmental and agricultural applications where she develops methods that are fit for purpose, relevant to the question at hand, and usable by decision-makers.
Her work, particularly supporting Great Barrier Reef decision-making, has been recognised through awards including 1st Runner Up (APAC Women in AI Innovator of the Year, 2023) and the APAC Women in AI Award for Environment and Biodiversity (2023).
A key contribution to AI-driven decision-making is her award-winning software Vizumap, an R package that helps users understand and communicate uncertainty on maps.
More recently, her focus has included machine-learning emulators to speed up slow-running physical system models, Bayesian methods for decision support, and approaches that use geospatial data (e.g., remote sensing) to improve prediction of terrestrial environmental and agricultural processes. Her previous roles include Associate Science Director for University Engagement and Group Leader of the Statistical Machine Learning Group in CSIRO’s Data61.
She has co-authored 100+ journal articles, with 6,000+ citations and a Google Scholar h-index of 30+. Her collaborations span leading government departments, universities and industry.

Along the way, I have developed some strong opinions about statistics and how statisticians work. I will discuss some of these. Her interests are in good data management practices, well-designed experiments, and in improving communication between statisticians and scientists.



Dr. Salvador Gezan


Presentation Title

Fitting Large Genomic Models: Computational Strategies and Approximations within the Linear Mixed Model Framework

Abstract

As genomic datasets grow larger, substantial statistical and computational challenges arise when analysing single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) data. Such data are widely used in Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS), Polygenic Risk Score (PRS) analyses, and genome-wide prediction models. Depending on the field and context, it is common to encounter datasets containing millions of SNPs and hundreds of thousands of genotyped individuals. Fitting even the simplest linear mixed model at this scale is computationally demanding, requiring the handling of large genomic matrices and the estimation of a large number of marker effects. Statistical and mathematical techniques such as Cholesky decomposition, eigen-transformation, Singular Value Decomposition, and low-rank matrix approximations provide practical solutions for fitting these models and obtaining the required effects and predictions. This talk will present key mathematical details, illustrations, and practical guidelines for addressing large-scale genomic analyses in plant and animal breeding.

Biography

Salvador Gezan is a statistician and quantitative geneticist with over 20 years of experience, currently serving as a Statistical Genetics Consultant at VSN International. He specialises in mixed models and their application to biological problems, supporting agricultural, forestry, and aquaculture breeding programmes through the analysis of phenotypic and genotypic data, the development of breeding strategies, and the implementation of genomic selection in operational breeding programmes. He began his career at Rothamsted Research, was an Associate Professor at the University of Florida, and has delivered ASReml workshops globally. Dr. Gezan has over 160 peer-reviewed publications and is a co-author of Statistical Methods in Biology: Design and Analysis of Experiments and Regression.
